knowledge_points.label: Raw data is HTML/PDF/repos; text extraction is lossy and its accuracy matters
knowledge_points.statement: Pretraining text does not arrive as text: HTML (the main case), PDFs and code directories must be linearized by rule-based extractors (trafilatura, resiliparse, jusText, lynx) that strip boilerplate and inevitably lose images, tables and layout, and the choice of extractor measurably changes downstream model quality.

anchors.quote: Raw data does not come as text. ... It is HTML, PDF (arxiv), or directories (code repositories).

HTML to text (main one): ... Remove boilerplate (e.g., navigation, ads) and extract content ... Inherently lossy (need to linearize) ... Tools (rule-based): trafilatura, resiliparse, jusText, lynx, etc. ... Accuracy matters
Recrawl truncated PDFs (since they are big) ... OCR (RolmOCR) using a VLM or Docling (make these run fast) ... A lot of layout information is missing

anchors.ref: post linked at L51, pipeline figure at L52

anchors.quote: So raw data doesn't come as text, even as if you've scraped something. ... It's either HTML. ... So most of the attention on transforming data is dealing with HTML because most of the web is in HTML.
So inherently, this is a lossy process because you need to linearize HTML ... Simple tables, you can render using markdown. ... But if you have nested tables, then that becomes quite challenging.
So, typically, HTML to text processing is rule-based. ... And the reason for this is that rule-based processors are very fast. ... You don't need too much intelligence.

And, some PDFs might be just scans as well. ... mostly this involves running OCR using a VLM. ... And this obviously can be much more expensive than what we were doing before with text. ... So the quality of an average PDF is generally higher than for HTML file.
in HTML you have various tags like h1 and p that gives you some semantic information. ... PDFs are, by design, all about layout.

provenance.filtering_note: The DCLM comparison of extractors (images/dclm-wet.png, L49) is the only evidence for 'Accuracy matters'; its accuracy numbers are inside the image and are not restated. The FinePDFs pipeline (Common Crawl source, recrawling truncated PDFs, RolmOCR or Docling, 'lots of cleanup and filtering', L51-L57) is given as a second linearization case and is folded here rather than made a KP: the professor states no mechanism beyond the bullet list. 'What about images, tables, etc.?' (L45) is left as a question. Spoken evidence (3:10-3:31): why extraction stays rule-based: 'rule-based processors are very fast' and the step does not need 'too much intelligence'; he allows 'a case for model-based interventions' if they are fast (3:34). Imperfections in extracted text are blamed on the failure rate of any rule-based processor (3:45). The DCLM figure is read aloud only as 'Resiliparse on these extended dclm evals works better than the others' (4:05); its numbers are still not restated. Correction (2:52-3:04): the note says 'What about images, tables, etc.?' is left as a question; aloud tables are partly answered: simple tables can be rendered as markdown, nested tables force you to 'give up at some point or approximate'. Images are not answered. Correction (5:24-6:34): the note says the professor states no mechanism for FinePDFs beyond the bullet list. Aloud: some PDFs are scans, so conversion means OCR with a VLM, 'much more expensive' than HTML extraction; PDFs are 'a very small fraction' of the web but of higher average quality ('if you bother to make a PDF ... you probably have something interesting to say'); and layout is lost because PDFs are 'by design, all about layout' while HTML tags like h1 and p carry semantic structure.

external_prerequisites.note: Common Crawl's WARC/WET distinction (raw HTML vs pre-extracted text) is the context in which 'accuracy matters' (L48) and the dclm-wet.png figure make sense.

misconceptions.belief: HTML-to-text extraction is a solved preprocessing step; any extractor gives the same training text.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The professor's one-line verdict is 'Accuracy matters' with the DCLM extractor comparison as evidence (L48-L49); extractors differ in how much boilerplate they leave and how much content they drop.

misconceptions.belief: A good extractor is lossless: it recovers the page's content exactly.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Extraction is 'inherently lossy (need to linearize)' (L46): images, tables and layout (L45, L57) have no faithful one-dimensional text form.

predict.q: Two teams build a web corpus from the same Common Crawl snapshot, differing only in the HTML-to-text extractor. Per the lecture's DCLM evidence, what happens to downstream model quality?
choices: It is unchanged: the same pages yield the same training text either way.
It differs measurably: extractors differ in boilerplate kept and content lost.
It differs only if one team also changes the quality filter afterwards.
It is unchanged: any good extractor recovers each page's content exactly.
predict.answer: It differs measurably: extractors differ in boilerplate kept and content lost.
predict.why: It differs measurably: the extractor changes how much boilerplate stays and how much content is lost. 'Accuracy matters' is the professor's summary of the DCLM extractor comparison (L48-L49); the extractor decides what the model ever sees.
predict.targets_misconception: HTML-to-text extraction is a solved preprocessing step; any extractor gives the same training text.
distractor_from: 'the same pages yield the same text' <- misconception: 'HTML-to-text extraction is a solved preprocessing step; any extractor gives the same training text.'
'any good extractor recovers content exactly' <- misconception: 'A good extractor is lossless: it recovers the page's content exactly.'
'only if the quality filter changes' <- plausible: treats extraction as separate from, and dominated by, filtering

transfer.q: A team linearizes arXiv PDFs with an OCR model and finds that equations and two-column layout come out scrambled. Which property of text extraction named in the lecture explains this, and why does switching from HTML to PDF not remove it?
transfer.answer: Extraction is inherently lossy because content must be linearized (L46); PDFs add OCR and lose 'a lot of layout information' (L55, L57), so the same loss appears in a different form rather than disappearing.
transfer.why: Both HTML and PDF are two-dimensional presentations; any text target forces a one-dimensional order, and the professor names lossiness as intrinsic, not as a defect of one tool.
transfer.varies: domain: the source format changes from HTML to PDF (arXiv), the lecture's secondary case
transfer.invariant: linearization loses layout regardless of the input format or the extractor

check.q: A web page's key content is a product-comparison table (rows of products, columns of specs). It is run through a rule-based HTML-to-text extractor such as trafilatura. Per the lecture, what does the extracted text keep?
choices: nothing of it, since rule-based extractors drop every table
the whole table, since a good extractor loses nothing
the cell text, but not the table's row and column structure
check.answer: the cell text, but not the table's row and column structure
check.why: L43-L48: HTML-to-text extraction removes boilerplate and extracts content but is 'inherently lossy (need to linearize)'; a 2D table becomes a 1D stream of its cell text, losing the layout that relates cells.
check.varies: the lost structure is an HTML table rather than PDF equations and two-column layout
check.invariant: extraction must linearize, so layout and structure are lost whatever the source format
check.targets_misconception: A good extractor is lossless: it recovers the page's content exactly.
distractor_from: 'the whole table, since a good extractor loses nothing' <- misconception: 'A good extractor is lossless: it recovers the page's content exactly.'
'nothing of it, since rule-based extractors drop every table' <- plausible: over-generalises 'remove boilerplate' to removing all non-paragraph content

knowledge_points.label: Filtering = given target T and raw R, find T' ⊂ R similar to T, fast and generalizing
knowledge_points.statement: Every filter in the lecture is one algorithmic building block: given a small target set T (what good looks like) and a huge raw set R, estimate a model from R and T, derive a score, and keep the R examples whose score passes a threshold; the algorithm must generalize beyond T (T' should differ from T) and be extremely fast because it runs over all of R.

anchors.quote: Algorithmic building block: ... Given some **target data** T and lots of **raw data** R, find subset T' of R similar to T.
Applications: ... Language identification (English versus rest) ... Quality filtering (high quality versus low quality) ... Toxicity filtering (non-toxic versus toxic)
Desiderata for filtering algorithm: ... Generalize from the target data (want T and T' to be different) ... Extremely fast (have to run it on R, which is huge)
General framework: Given target T and raw R, find subset of R similar to T ... 1. Estimate some model based on R and T and derive a scoring function ... 2. Keep examples in R based on their score
Filtering is critical for building a good model ... Recipe: define target data (what good looks like), extrapolate to raw data
Here's the building block. ... This is usually a small amount of high-quality data and lots of raw data. ... And the goal is to find a subset of this raw data that is similar to target.

for a filtering algorithm, you want some generalization from the target data, because you already have the target data. ... So this could be 100 trillion tokens worth of data. ... a single-digit fraction of your entire data.
So the general scheme is that you estimate some model based on R and T and derive a scoring function, and then you keep the examples in R based on their score.

provenance.filtering_note: The schema figure images/raw-target-schema.png (L63) is shown without numbers. The survey (L74) is a pointer only. The professor frames language ID, quality and toxicity as the same problem with different T (L65-L68); the specific classifiers are the next KPs. 'Stochastically' at L83 is treated under pareto-stochastic-keep. Spoken evidence (8:18-8:53): the reason T' must differ from T is said: 'because you already have the target data'; the speed requirement gets a size, R 'could be 100 trillion tokens'; and he estimates that filtering keeps 'a single-digit fraction' of the data (no number in the code). The closing summary (21:56-22:54) says filtering matters most when compute-constrained ('if you have infinite compute, you don't need to filter') and gives two ways to get T: an existing dataset 'I really like', or a prompted LM that pre-filters a pool to train a smaller classifier (anchored on quality-positives-define-quality).

external_prerequisites.note: R in every example is Common Crawl (L98, L106, L114); its size is why 'extremely fast' (L72) is a hard constraint.

misconceptions.belief: A quality filter's job is to find more documents like the target set, so the ideal output T' equals T.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The first desideratum is to 'generalize from the target data (want T and T' to be different)' (L71): T is a definition of good, not the corpus to be recovered.

misconceptions.belief: Filtering accuracy matters more than filtering speed, so a large model should score every page.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The second desideratum is 'extremely fast (have to run it on R, which is huge)' (L72); the lecture's scorers are a KenLM and a fastText linear model (L81-L82), not large LMs.

predict.q: A team's quality filter returns exactly the Wikipedia pages it was given as T and nothing else from Common Crawl. Per the two desiderata, which one has it failed?
choices: Generalization: T' should differ from T.
Speed: it must run over all of R.
Neither: returning T is the ideal result.
predict.answer: Generalization: T' should differ from T.
predict.why: L71 says the algorithm must 'generalize from the target data (want T and T' to be different)'; the point is to find new good data in R.
predict.targets_misconception: A quality filter's job is to find more documents like the target set, so the ideal output T' equals T.
predict.distractor_from: Option 3 from 'ideal T' equals T'; option 2 from confusing a precision failure with a cost failure.

transfer.q: You want a corpus of legal contracts from a 100-billion-page web crawl and have 5,000 hand-checked contracts. Map this onto the lecture's framework: what are T and R, which of the two desiderata is the binding one here, and what does that rule out?
transfer.answer: T = the 5,000 checked contracts, R = the crawl. The binding desideratum is speed (the scorer runs on 100B pages), which rules out scoring each page with a large LM; the scorer must be cheap (a KenLM or fastText-style model estimated from T and R), while still generalizing beyond the 5,000 so T' is new contracts, not the seed set.
transfer.why: The framework is domain-agnostic: estimate a model from R and T, derive a score, keep by score (L76-L78), under the two desiderata (L71-L72).
transfer.varies: domain: the target changes from language/quality/toxicity to a legal genre
transfer.invariant: the T/R decomposition and the speed constraint set by the size of R

check.q: The lecture's filter must run over all of R. Suppose instead R is 20,000 candidate documents and T is 300 hand-picked examples. Which of the two filtering desiderata stops constraining the choice of scorer?
choices: neither: both desiderata still bind whatever the size of R
generalization: T' is now allowed to be the same as T
extreme speed: scoring 20,000 documents is cheap anyway
check.answer: extreme speed: scoring 20,000 documents is cheap anyway
check.why: L70-L72: the filter must be extremely fast because it runs on R, which is huge. With R at 20,000 documents even a large-model scorer is affordable, so speed no longer binds; generalizing beyond T (T' different from T) still matters.
check.varies: R is tiny instead of a 100B-page crawl (inverse direction: when does speed stop binding)
check.invariant: speed binds because the scorer runs over all of R; generalization binds because T' should differ from T
check.targets_misconception: Filtering accuracy matters more than filtering speed, so a large model should score every page.
distractor_from: 'generalization: T' is now allowed to be the same as T' <- misconception: 'A quality filter's job is to find more documents like the target set, so the ideal output T' equals T.'
'neither: both desiderata still bind whatever the size of R' <- plausible: treats the desiderata as fixed rules rather than consequences of R's size

retrieval.q: In the professor's notation, what are T, R and T'?
retrieval.answer: T is the target data, R the raw data, T' the subset of R similar to T.

retrieval.q: State the two desiderata for a filtering algorithm.
retrieval.answer: Generalize from the target data (T and T' should differ) and be extremely fast (it runs on all of R).

retrieval.q: What are the two steps of the general filtering framework?
retrieval.answer: Estimate a model from R and T to derive a scoring function; keep examples in R based on their score.

knowledge_points.label: Two scorers: generative p_T(x) (KenLM perplexity) vs discriminative p(T | x) (fastText)
knowledge_points.statement: The score can come from a generative model of the target alone, score(x) = p_T(x) (a KenLM n-gram model, used as a perplexity cutoff), or from a simple classifier trained on T against R, score(x) = p(T | x) (fastText); OpenMathText uses both, keeping pages with ProofPile-KenLM perplexity below 15000 and a fastText math classifier with a threshold of 0.17 if the page has math and 0.8 if not.

anchors.quote: Types of classifiers: ... Generative model of T (KenLM): score(x) = p_T(x) ... Simple classifier (fastText): score(x) = p(T | x) ... To use: keep examples x with score(x) >= threshold (stochastically)
Model-based filtering? ... Some deliberately do not use model-based filtering (C4, Gopher, RefinedWeb, FineWeb, Dolma) ... Some use model-based filtering (GPT-3, LLaMA, DCLM) [becoming the norm]

Goal: curate large corpus of mathematical text from CommonCrawl ... Use rules to filter (e.g., contains latex commands) ... KenLM trained on ProofPile, keep if perplexity < 15000 ... Trained fastText classifier to predict mathematical writing, threshold is 0.17 if math, 0.8 if no math
Result: produced 14.7B tokens, used to train 1.4B models that do better than models trained on 20x data

So typically, there are two types of classifiers. ... One are generative models. ... And remember, this has to be cheap, so probably you're not training a big language model. ... Generally, KenLM basically says I'm going to train a 5-gram model.

A more common thing, which I think we're mostly seeing these days, is just training a classifier. ... So basically, it looks like T are your positive examples, some random subset of R are your negative examples. ... And the tool that people generally use is fastText because it's fast.

there are many data sets from generally a few years ago that did not use model-based filtering because they wanted to not bias things too much. ... These days, I think basically everyone does some amount of model-based filtering

They also use KenLM. ... So this is a generative approach. ... And there's two different thresholds if it has latex in it, then it's a higher bar-- sorry-- it's a lower bar, but if it doesn't have latex in it, it's a higher bar.
And then, as a result, they got 15 billion tokens, which they use to train models. ... better at math than models that were trained on 20 times as much data

provenance.filtering_note: The professor labels arXiv 2310.06786 'OpenMathText'; the paper's own title is OpenWebMath (sources.json). The perplexity cutoff 15000, the 0.17/0.8 thresholds, '14.7B tokens' and 'better than models trained on 20x data' (L100-L102) are that paper's numbers as read by the professor and are quoted, not asserted. The professor does not explain why the math-present threshold (0.17) is looser than the no-math threshold (0.8); this thread reads it as a rule-based prior (L99: 'contains latex commands') relaxing the classifier, and marks that reading as inference. The list of datasets that avoid model-based filtering (L86) is context; it is the hinge for this KP's second misconception. Spoken evidence (9:13-10:26): KenLM is 'a 5-gram model', chosen because the scorer 'has to be cheap'; the classifier's negatives are 'some random subset of R', 'maybe you balance it'; fastText is used 'because it's fast' and is 'a linear classifier-- a bag of words'. Why some datasets skip model-based filtering is said (10:46): 'they wanted to not bias things too much'; why most now filter (10:59-11:18): unless you are 'compute-plentiful' you waste FLOPs on low-quality content. Correction, partial (13:38-13:51): the note says the professor does not explain the looser 0.17 threshold; he still gives no reason, but he states the condition: 'if it has latex in it ... it's a lower bar', which matches this thread's reading of L101's 'if math' as L99's LaTeX rule (self-corrected from 'higher bar' in the same sentence). '15 billion tokens' (13:51) rounds L102's 14.7B; the 1.4B model size is not said. Flag (10:59): aloud, 'These days, I think basically everyone does some amount of model-based filtering', which is stronger than L87's 'becoming the norm'; so the second misconception was restated (2026-10-02) to a belief that stays false: that the older corpora skipped classifiers for cost, when they skipped them to avoid bias.

prerequisites.note: The two scorers are the two ways to 'estimate some model based on R and T' (L77).

external_prerequisites.note: CCNet's KenLM-perplexity-on-Wikipedia filter is the canonical generative scorer; the lecture reuses KenLM here (L81, L100).

misconceptions.belief: A KenLM perplexity filter and a fastText classifier are two implementations of the same thing: both estimate how likely a page is to be from T.
misconceptions.why_wrong: KenLM scores p_T(x), the probability of the text under a model of T alone, and never sees R; fastText scores p(T | x), which needs negatives from R and measures how T-like versus R-like a page is (L81-L82). A page can be fluent (low perplexity) yet not T-like, and vice versa.

misconceptions.belief: Corpora such as C4, RefinedWeb, FineWeb and Dolma skipped model-based filtering only because they could not afford to train a classifier.
misconceptions.why_wrong: They skipped it on purpose: C4, Gopher, RefinedWeb, FineWeb and Dolma 'deliberately do not use model-based filtering' (L86), and the professor gives the reason aloud (10:46-11:18): 'because they wanted to not bias things too much'. A fastText classifier is cheap to train; the cost is the bias toward whatever T is. He adds that today 'basically everyone does some amount of model-based filtering', which is why GPT-3, LLaMA and DCLM-style pipelines are 'becoming the norm' (L87).

predict.q: A page is a fluently written cooking blog. T is mathematical text (ProofPile), R is Common Crawl. Which scorer is more likely to let it through, and why?
choices: The KenLM filter: fluent English gets moderate perplexity regardless of topic.
The fastText classifier: trained on T alone, it scores fluent text as T-like.
Both equally: both scorers estimate p_T(x), the probability under T.
Neither: both are trained to separate T from R, so a blog fails both.
predict.answer: The KenLM filter: fluent English gets moderate perplexity regardless of topic.
predict.why: The KenLM perplexity filter, because fluent English can have moderate perplexity under any English-ish n-gram model regardless of topic. KenLM scores p_T(x) with no negatives (L81); fastText is trained to separate T from R (L82), so an ordinary blog is a typical negative and is rejected. This is why OpenMathText stacks both (L100-L101).
predict.targets_misconception: A KenLM perplexity filter and a fastText classifier are two implementations of the same thing: both estimate how likely a page is to be from T.
distractor_from: 'Both equally: both estimate p_T(x)' <- misconception: 'A KenLM perplexity filter and a fastText classifier are two implementations of the same thing'
'Neither: both separate T from R' <- same misconception, from the discriminative side
'The fastText classifier, trained on T alone' <- plausible: forgets that a discriminative classifier needs negatives from R

transfer.q: You are filtering for Swahili legal text. You have 2 GB of Swahili statutes but no labelled negatives yet. Which of the two scorer types can you build today, what does its score mean, and what failure should you expect until you add negatives?
transfer.answer: Only the generative scorer (a KenLM on the statutes), whose score is p_T(x): the likelihood of the page under a model of the target alone. Until negatives from R are added to train a p(T | x) classifier, it will pass any fluent Swahili text that resembles the statutes' n-gram statistics (news, other formal prose), because low perplexity does not mean T-like rather than R-like.
transfer.why: The generative scorer needs only T (L81); the discriminative one needs T and R (L82). The failure mode is the gap between 'likely under T' and 'more T than R'.
transfer.varies: domain and functional: a new language and genre, and the question is which scorer is constructible from available data
transfer.invariant: p_T(x) needs only target data; p(T | x) needs target and raw negatives

both: perplexity is measured against R
only B: it is trained on T against R

retrieval.answer: Generative: score(x) = p_T(x), KenLM. Discriminative: score(x) = p(T | x), fastText.

knowledge_points.label: Off-the-shelf filters inherit their training domain: fastText langid, Jigsaw toxicity
knowledge_points.statement: Language ID and toxicity filtering reuse off-the-shelf classifiers whose notion of 'English' or 'toxic' is the one in their training data: fastText langid covers 176 languages but learned them from Wikipedia, Tatoeba and SETimes, and Dolma keeps pages with p(English) >= 0.5; Dolma's toxicity filter is trained on the 2018 Jigsaw dataset of Wikipedia talk-page comments labelled {toxic, severe_toxic, obscene, threat, insult, identity_hate}, so what each filter removes is defined by those corpora, not by the pretraining target.

anchors.quote: Language identification: ... Goal: find text of a specific language (e.g., English) ... Off-the-shelf classifier ... Supports 176 languages ... Trained on multilingual sites: Wikipedia, Tatoeba (translation site) and SETimes (Southeast European news) ... Dolma keeps pages with p(English) >= 0.5

Toxicity filtering in Dolma ... Dataset: Jigsaw Toxic Comments dataset (2018) ... Project goal: help people have better discussions online ... Data: comments on Wikipedia talk page annotated with {toxic, severe_toxic, obscene, threat, insult, identity_hate}

anchors.ref: paper linked at L95 and L129

anchors.quote: So Meta has trained this set of fastText language identification models, which often you can just use off the shelf. ... So it supports 176 different languages. ... So Wikipedia, remember, has a lot of languages.
So a language ID is generally a fairly easy problem ... Now, there are subtleties because of code-switching and text, and there's some dialects. ... This is generally fairly heuristic.
So toxicity works the same way. ... So here the data is the Wikipedia talk pages, which can, I guess, for controversial sites get quite heated.

provenance.filtering_note: The professor states the training sources of both classifiers but does not himself say 'this is a bias'; the inference that a filter's removals are shaped by its training domain (e.g., short, informal, code-mixed or dialectal English scoring below 0.5; talk-page notions of toxicity flagging other registers) is this thread's reading, marked basis=inference in the misconceptions. Correction, partial (12:19-12:25): the note says the professor does not himself say 'this is a bias' and that the code-mixed or dialectal failure cases are this thread's reading. He does not tie those failures to the training corpora; that link stays this thread's. transfer.q: A medical-forum corpus is filtered with a toxicity classifier trained on Wikipedia talk-page comments. Posts describing symptoms with anatomical terms start disappearing. Using the lecture's description of the Jigsaw data, explain what the filter is actually removing and name the general principle.
transfer.answer: It is removing text that resembles what talk-page moderators labelled {toxic, severe_toxic, obscene, threat, insult, identity_hate} (L132), and anatomical terms are 'obscene' in that register. The principle: an off-the-shelf filter's definition of the unwanted class is the one in its training corpus, so what it removes from a new domain is a bias inherited from that corpus, not a property of the new domain.
transfer.why: Every filter is p(T | x) for some T; when T is a borrowed labelled set, the filter's removals follow that set's labelling conventions (L129-L132).
transfer.varies: domain: medical forum instead of general web; the filter is applied to a register absent from its training data
transfer.invariant: the classifier's notion of the class is fixed by its training labels

knowledge_points.label: Quality classifiers: the positive set is the definition of quality (GPT-3, LLaMA, phi-1)
knowledge_points.statement: A quality filter is a classifier whose positives define 'quality' and whose negatives are Common Crawl: GPT-3 used {Wikipedia, WebText2, Books1, Books2} and a linear word-feature classifier kept stochastically; LLaMA/RedPajama used pages referenced by Wikipedia and kept classified positives; phi-1 used GPT-4 to label 100K Stack-Python files for educational value, trained a random forest on codegen embeddings, and reports that the filtered subset trained a better 1.3B model with fewer steps.

anchors.quote: Positives: samples from {Wikipedia, WebText2, Books1, Books2} ... Negatives: samples from CommonCrawl ... Train linear classifier based on word features ... Keep documents stochastically based on score
Positives: samples from pages **referenced** by Wikipedia ... Negatives: samples from CommonCrawl ... Keep documents that are classified positive

Philosophy: really high quality data (textbooks) to train a small model (1.5B) ... determine its educational value for a student whose goal is to learn basic coding concepts ... Use GPT-4 with this prompt to classify 100K subset of R to get positive examples ... Train random forest classifier on T using output embedding from pretrained codegen model
Train 1.3B LM on Python subset of The Stack (performance: 12.19% after 96K steps) ... Train 1.3B LM on new filtered subset (performance: 17.68% after 36K steps) - better!
So the quality filtering again, think about it as a tool. ... You can define quality however you want. ... There's no universal notion of quality.
So positive examples are Wikipedia, WebText. ... So these are pages that link out from high-star Reddit posts, and some books. ... And negatives are generally sampled from the web.

And they define a prompt, which determines educational value. ... So the target here is actually the output of an expensive classifier. ... in their case, a Random Forest, but you could have probably used fastText as well.

So the recipe here is figure out what good data looks like. ... Or you can craft a prompt to a language model and then use that to construct, to do a preliminary filter of a large pool, and then use that good quality data to train a smaller classifier

provenance.filtering_note: The HumanEval numbers 12.19% (96K steps) and 17.68% (36K steps) are phi-1's as read by the professor (L126-L127) and are quoted, not asserted. The phi-1 R/prompt/T are Python string variables (L120-L122), not text() calls; they are quoted from the source. The professor says LLaMA keeps 'classified positive' (L115) without a threshold; GPT-3's stochastic rule is its own KP (pareto-stochastic-keep). That each positive set is a different, contestable definition of quality (encyclopedic/book prose, Wikipedia-citable pages, GPT-4's idea of educational code) is the professor's implicit contrast; the word 'bias' is this thread's. Correction (14:13-14:21): the note calls the contrast between positive sets 'the professor's implicit contrast'. It is explicit: 'You can define quality however you want. There's no universal notion of quality. If you want to define quality to be math, then you can go and get math.' (The word 'bias' is still this thread's.) Spoken evidence: WebText is glossed as 'pages that link out from high-star Reddit posts' (14:36); phi-1's target is 'the output of an expensive classifier' distilled into a cheap one, and fastText 'could have probably' replaced the random forest (15:55-16:01); the closing recipe names the two sources of T, an existing dataset or a prompted LM whose labels train a smaller classifier (22:28-22:54). The HumanEval numbers are not read aloud ('performance goes up in fewer steps to a higher value', 16:25).

prerequisites.note: Each positive set is a concrete T; Common Crawl is R (L105-L106, L113-L114).
All three are discriminative p(T | x) scorers (linear word features, fastText-style, random forest).

external_prerequisites.note: GPT-3's data sources (WebText2, Books1/2) were introduced in lecture 13; here they reappear as the classifier's positives.

misconceptions.why_wrong: Each recipe chooses its positives: GPT-3 picks Wikipedia/WebText2/Books (L105), LLaMA picks pages referenced by Wikipedia (L113), phi-1 picks what GPT-4 calls educational for 'basic coding concepts' (L121-L122). Different positives, different corpora; the classifier only extrapolates the chosen definition to R.

misconceptions.belief: Filtering harder always costs performance because you train on fewer tokens.
misconceptions.why_wrong: phi-1's filtered subset reached 17.68% HumanEval after 36K steps versus 12.19% after 96K on the unfiltered Python Stack, as read from the paper (L126-L127): fewer, more targeted tokens and fewer steps.

The GPT-3-style one: WebText (Reddit-linked pages, many blogs) and books resemble the post; Wikipedia-cited pages are mostly news and reference.
The LLaMA-style classifier: pages Wikipedia cites span every topic, so its positives are broader and it keeps more well-written pages of any kind.

'The LLaMA-style classifier' <- plausible: assumes the broader-looking positive set is more permissive

transfer.q: A team wants a pretraining corpus for a children's-reading-level model. They copy phi-1's recipe but label their 100K positives with the prompt 'rate this page's literary merit'. Predict what the resulting filter keeps, and state what in the recipe they should have changed.
transfer.answer: It keeps pages that an LLM judges to have literary merit (sophisticated prose), not pages a child can read, because the positive set T is the operational definition of quality that the classifier extrapolates to R. They should have changed the labelling prompt to the actual target ('readable by a 7-year-old'), as phi-1 did with 'educational value for a student whose goal is to learn basic coding concepts' (L121).
transfer.why: In every recipe quality = membership in the positive set (L105, L113, L121-L122); the classifier cannot correct a mis-specified T.
transfer.varies: domain and functional: a new target audience, and the question is about the labelling prompt rather than the classifier
transfer.invariant: the positive set defines what the filter calls quality

check.q: A team copies GPT-3's quality classifier (Common Crawl negatives, linear word features) but swaps its positives from {Wikipedia, WebText2, Books1, Books2} to a corpus of court opinions. knowledge_points.label: GPT-3's stochastic keep: keep iff Pareto(9) sample > 1 − score
knowledge_points.statement: GPT-3 does not threshold its quality score; it keeps a document when a draw from np.random.pareto(9) exceeds 1 − score, so high-scoring documents are almost always kept while low-scoring ones are kept with small but nonzero probability (evaluating numpy's Pareto tail gives P(keep) = (2 − score)^−9: 1.0 at score 1, about 0.42 at 0.9, about 0.026 at 0.5, about 0.002 at 0), which preserves some diversity from the low-score mass.

anchors.quote: Keep documents stochastically based on score ... def keep_document(score: float) -> bool: ... return np.random.pareto(9) > 1 - score
To use: keep examples x with score(x) >= threshold (stochastically)

And then once you have this model now for every new document, you can score it, and you set some appropriate threshold, depending on your quality bar, and you keep the examples. ... Sometimes stochastically, sometimes not.
They train a linear classifier and keep documents if the linear classifier is scored highly enough.

provenance.filtering_note: The function at L109-L110 is defined but never called and carries no @inspect, so the lecture shows no keep probabilities. The closed form P(keep | score) = (2 − score)^−9 is this thread's derivation from numpy's documented Pareto (Lomax) tail P(X > x) = (1 + x)^−9 for x >= 0, with x = 1 − score; a 2e6-draw Monte Carlo in this thread matched it to three digits (0.0020, 0.0065, 0.026, 0.134, 0.424, 1.0 at scores 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9, 1). Status is 'said' with basis 'inference' because the professor states only the rule. The professor does not say why stochastic rather than hard thresholding; 'diversity' is this thread's reading, consistent with his later mixing remark about ensuring diversity (L352). Spoken (10:26-10:41): the only spoken trace of stochastic keeping is 'Sometimes stochastically, sometimes not'. keep_document and np.random.pareto(9) (L109-L110) are never discussed aloud, so a video-only learner meets this KP only through the code; no reason for stochastic keeping is given aloud either. Spoken slip (14:47): GPT-3 is described as keeping documents 'if the linear classifier is scored highly enough', which reads as a hard threshold; L108 says 'Keep documents stochastically based on score'. Not imported.

prerequisites.note: The score is the GPT-3 linear classifier's output (L107); the keep rule follows at L108-L110.

misconceptions.belief: Documents below the quality threshold are discarded; 'stochastically' just means the threshold is noisy.
misconceptions.why_wrong: There is no threshold: every score has a nonzero keep probability (2 − score)^−9 (derived from L110), about 1 in 500 even at score 0, so some low-scoring documents are always kept.

misconceptions.belief: A document with score 0.5 is kept about half the time.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The rule keeps iff Pareto(9) > 0.5, which has probability 1.5^−9 ≈ 0.026 (derived from L110); the Pareto tail with shape 9 is steep, so keep probability collapses quickly below score 1.

predict.q: Under GPT-3's keep rule, a document with classifier score 0.9 and one with score 0.5 arrive. Roughly how do their keep probabilities compare?
choices: About 0.9 vs 0.5: the classifier score is the keep probability.
About 0.42 vs 0.026: the Pareto(9) tail falls as (1 + x)^−9.
Both 1.0: anything above a 0.5 threshold is kept, with noise.
predict.answer: About 0.42 vs 0.026: the Pareto(9) tail falls as (1 + x)^−9.
predict.why: About 0.42 vs 0.026: more than 15x apart, because the Pareto(9) tail falls as (1 + x)^−9. Keep iff Pareto(9) > 1 − score (L110); P = (2 − score)^−9 gives 1.1^−9 ≈ 0.42 and 1.5^−9 ≈ 0.026 (this thread's evaluation of the rule).
predict.targets_misconception: A document with score 0.5 is kept about half the time.
distractor_from: 'About 0.9 vs 0.5' <- misconception: 'A document with score 0.5 is kept about half the time.'
'Both 1.0, threshold with noise' <- misconception: 'Documents below the quality threshold are discarded; 'stochastically' just means the threshold is noisy.'

transfer.q: An engineer replaces Pareto(9) with Pareto(3) in the same rule to 'be less strict'. Before computing, predict the direction of change for low-scoring documents and say why; then give the keep probability at score 0 under each shape.
transfer.answer: Low-scoring documents are kept far more often: a smaller shape parameter gives a heavier tail, so P(X > 1 − score) rises for every score < 1. At score 0: 2^−9 ≈ 0.002 with shape 9 versus 2^−3 = 0.125 with shape 3, about 64x more junk admitted.
transfer.why: P(keep) = (2 − score)^−a from the Lomax tail (1 + x)^−a; the exponent a controls how fast keep probability decays away from score 1.
transfer.varies: functional: the Pareto shape parameter changes; the rule's form is unchanged
transfer.invariant: keep iff a heavy-tailed draw exceeds 1 − score; monotone in score, nonzero everywhere

check.q: numpy's np.random.pareto(a) draws X with P(X > x) = (1 + x)^-a. GPT-3 keeps a document when np.random.pareto(9) > 1 - score. What classifier score gives a keep probability of exactly 0.5? Give the score as a decimal to two places.
check.why: P(keep) = P(X > 1 - s) = (2 - s)^-9. Setting (2 - s)^-9 = 0.5 gives 2 - s = 2^(1/9) = 1.0801, so s = 0.920. A score of 0.5 is kept only about 2.6% of the time, not half the time.
check.varies: inverse direction: given a keep probability, find the score (instead of changing the shape parameter)
check.invariant: keep probability = Pareto(9) tail at 1 - score = (2 - score)^-9
check.targets_misconception: A document with score 0.5 is kept about half the time.

retrieval.q: What keep probability does the rule give at score 1, and roughly at score 0 (derived)?
retrieval.answer: 1.0 at score 1; about 2^−9 ≈ 0.002 at score 0.

prompts.self_explain: Why might a corpus builder want a few low-scoring documents to survive rather than cutting cleanly at a threshold?

presentations.ref: P(keep | score) = P(Pareto(9) > 1 − score) = (1 + (1 − score))^−9 = (2 − score)^−9

steps.do: Keep iff X > 1 − score, with X drawn from np.random.pareto(9) (L110).
steps.why: A random draw replaces the hard threshold, so every score keeps some chance of getting through.
np.random.pareto draws a Lomax variable (a Pareto shifted to start at 0), and this is its tail.
The keep probability is 1 at score 1 and falls fast below it.
The ninth power turns a small gap in score into a large gap in keep probability; the score is not the keep probability.

presentations.notice: The keep probability is not the score: it falls steeply below score 1 but never reaches 0, unlike the dashed hard threshold, so a few low-score documents always get through.

knowledge_points.label: No single optimal filter threshold: longer training wants more, lower-quality data
knowledge_points.statement: How aggressively to filter depends on how long you will train: a short run is best served by a small, high-quality subset, while a long run needs more tokens and should admit lower-quality data, so the optimal threshold moves with the training budget rather than being a property of the data.

anchors.quote: Scale-dependent effects of filtering: ... No single optimal threshold for filtering ... If training for longer, want more (lower quality) data ... If training for shorter, want less (higher quality) data

I want to talk about one subtlety here ... the notion of what you want for data actually depends on what model you want to train. ... So in particular, it depends on the number of tokens you're training on. ... And so there's no optimal threshold.
Intuitively, if you are going to train for a longer period of time, then you can tolerate lower quality data. ... The data pool is what it is.
So here's a preliminary experiment that Michael Ryan did. ... So basically, this plot shows for a 157-million parameter model.
And each of these lines is when you epoch over the data. ... So eventually, you have to repeat your data. ... And at some point, you start to overfit.

Whereas if you look at Resiliparse, this is basically no filtering. ... So you see this trend where high-quality data is better in this regime, where you're not epoching. ... But even at this point, this is worse than if you had trained for longer using low-quality data.
Ideally, that would be a good practice. ... But in reality, when we have done these experiments, it's generally tends to be stable, I would say, at least for pre-training.

provenance.filtering_note: The figure at L138 carries the evidence (curves of performance vs filtering aggressiveness at several training budgets); its numbers and its originating paper are not named in the lecture and are not restated. The professor does not connect this explicitly to repeated epochs over a small filtered set; this thread draws that link in the misconception and marks it inference, since the same mechanism is made explicit in data_mixing() at L353 and L365. Correction (18:23-20:14): the note says the figure's numbers and originating paper are not named and that the professor does not connect the effect to repeated epochs. Aloud the figure is 'a preliminary experiment that Michael Ryan did' (a 157M-parameter model on a small pool; the pool size is captioned '100 works', probably 100 WARC files, and is not restated), the blue curve is DCLM-filtered data and Resiliparse is 'basically no filtering'. He makes the epoch link explicit: each marker is an epoch, high-quality data is better 'in this regime, where you're not epoching', and even stopped early it ends 'worse than if you had trained for longer using low-quality data'. The misconception's epoch reading is therefore spoken evidence, not only inference. Spoken evidence: the magic-wand caveat (more high-quality data would be better still, 'but that's not an option ... The data pool is what it is', 18:10-18:20); Q&A (20:15-21:08): each point is a single run, and such pre-training ablations 'tend to be stable'; Q&A (21:30-21:46): a better dataset would also hit diminishing returns, only lower. The summary adds the compute framing: with infinite compute 'you don't need to filter' (22:05).

misconceptions.belief: There is a best quality threshold for a dataset; find it once at small scale and reuse it.
misconceptions.why_wrong: 'No single optimal threshold for filtering' (L135): the small-scale optimum is a strict threshold (L137) and the large-run optimum is a looser one (L136), because a long run exhausts the strictly filtered set (inference; see L353 for the epoching mechanism).

misconceptions.belief: More filtering is always better as long as enough tokens remain for one epoch.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The professor's rule is directional: the longer the training, the more lower-quality data you want (L136); the trade is between quality per token and token count, and the balance shifts with budget.

predict.q: A team tunes its quality threshold on 1B-token pilot runs and finds strict filtering wins. They then train a 2T-token model with the same threshold. Per the lecture, which way is the chosen threshold likely wrong?
choices: Too loose: large models are more sensitive to junk.
Too strict: training for longer wants more, lower-quality data than the short pilot preferred.
Not wrong: the optimal threshold is a property of the data, not the run.
predict.answer: Too strict: training for longer wants more, lower-quality data than the short pilot preferred.
predict.why: L136-L137: shorter runs favour less, higher-quality data; longer runs favour more, lower-quality data. The pilot's optimum does not transfer.
predict.targets_misconception: There is a best quality threshold for a dataset; find it once at small scale and reuse it.
predict.distractor_from: Option 3 from the 'property of the data' misconception; option 1 from the intuition that bigger models need cleaner data.

transfer.q: A fine-tuning team has 50M tokens of domain text and will train for only 20M tokens. Using the lecture's scale rule in reverse, should they filter their 50M aggressively or lightly, and what is the reason?
transfer.answer: Aggressively: a short run (20M tokens, less than one pass over 50M) is the 'training for shorter' case, which wants less, higher-quality data (L137); token count is not binding, so quality per token should dominate the choice.
transfer.why: The rule ties the threshold to the ratio of training budget to available data; when budget is well below supply, there is room to be strict.
transfer.varies: domain and functional: fine-tuning scale instead of pretraining, and the budget is below the data size rather than above it
transfer.invariant: the threshold trades quality per token against token count, and the budget decides which matters

check.q: A lab planned a 5T-token run and set a light quality filter. Its compute is then cut so the same model will train for only 500B tokens. Per the lecture's scale rule, which way should the fraction of the raw pool it keeps move? Start with up, down or same.
check.answer: Down: a shorter run wants less, higher-quality data, so the lab should filter harder and keep a smaller fraction of the pool.
check.why: L134-L137: there is no single optimal threshold; training for longer wants more (lower-quality) data and training for shorter wants less (higher-quality) data, so a 10x shorter run should keep a smaller, higher-quality fraction.
check.varies: the run gets shorter after the threshold was set, with pretraining-scale numbers instead of a small fine-tuning set
check.invariant: the optimal filter threshold moves with the training budget
check.targets_misconception: There is a best quality threshold for a dataset; find it once at small scale and reuse it.

knowledge_points.label: Dedup design space (item, match, action) and exact dedup by fast hashing in linear time
knowledge_points.statement: A deduplication scheme is three choices, what the item is (sentence, paragraph, document), how to match (exact, shared sub-item, fraction of sub-items) and what action to take (remove all, keep one); exact dedup hashes every item with a fast non-cryptographic hash (MurmurHash), groups by hash and keeps one per group, which is linear time and MapReduce-parallel but misses near duplicates, and C4 applies it to 3-sentence spans at the cost of document coherence.

anchors.quote: Two types of duplicates: ... Exact duplicates (mirror sites, GitHub forks) ... Near duplicates: same text differing by a few tokens

Product description repeated 61,036 times in C4 ... Deduplication training data makes language models better ... Train more efficiently (because have fewer tokens) ... Avoid memorization (can mitigate copyright, privacy concerns)

Design space: ... 1. What is an item (sentence, paragraph, document)? ... 2. How to match (exact match, existence of common subitem, fraction of common subitems)? ... 3. What action to take (remove all, remove all but one)? ... Deduplication is fundamentally about comparing items to other items ... Need linear time algorithms to scale

Tradeoff between efficiency and collision resistance ... Cryptographic hash functions (SHA-256): collision resistant, slow (used in bitcoin) ... DJB2, MurmurHash, CityHash: not collision resistant, fast (used for hash tables)

items = ["Hello!", "hello", "hello there", "hello", "hi", "bye"] ... hash_items = itertools.groupby(sorted(items, key=mmh3.hash), key=mmh3.hash) ... deduped_items = [next(group) for h, group in hash_items]

Pro: simple, clear semantics, high precision ... Con: does not deduplicate near duplicates ... This code is written in a MapReduce way, can easily parallelize and scale ... Item: 3-sentence spans ... Warning: when a 3-sentence span is removed from the middle of a document, the resulting document might not be coherent
There's exact duplicates. ... the whole point of a mirror is that it's a duplicate. ... Also, when you fork a repo, that is also a duplicate, even if you make changes.

So terms of service and licenses. ... And so in many cases, it is a exact copy, but only of that license, unless someone made a typo when they copied it. ... But the rest of the page that the license might be part of might be different.
So this audit of the C4 data set found this product description 61,000 times in the data set. ... So yeah, the web is weird.

So why deduplicate? ... Deduplication reduces your data set size without really losing information because you're just removing duplicates. ... But mostly, I think, it's just to make sure that you're not wasting flops.

the key algorithmic challenge is that deduplication is fundamentally about comparing items to other items. ... But your duplication, clearly, you can't do the n-squared thing where you compare everything to everything.
there are really fancy hash functions which are cryptographic in nature. ... And then there's these faster ones, which are used for hash tables, where hash collisions aren't the end of the world.
The items they operate on were three-sentence spans ... that means you're just going to rip out three sentences from that documents, which is a little bit strange, because it breaks the coherence.

provenance.filtering_note: The @inspect values h = mmh3.hash('hello') (L188) and deduped_items (L204) require the mmh3 library, which is not installed here, so neither is restated. What the code guarantees without running it: the two identical 'hello' strings hash identically and collapse to one, while 'Hello!' and 'hello there' are distinct strings and survive, so deduped_items has five strings in order of their hash values. '61,036 times in C4' (L155) is Lee et al.'s finding as read by the professor. The 'used in bitcoin' aside (L184) and the Gutenberg mirrors, MIT license and Amazon example links (L147, L151, L157) are illustrations, not mechanism. Spoken evidence (27:50-28:23): why deduplication needs hashing when filtering does not: filtering judges one item at a time, which 'can be parallelized' in linear time, while dedup compares items to each other and 'you can't do the n-squared thing'. The reasons to dedup are ranked aloud: efficiency first, memorization (copyright, privacy) second, 'mostly ... not wasting flops' (26:19-26:48); non-cryptographic hashes are fine because for hash tables 'hash collisions aren't the end of the world' (29:20). The mmh3 values (L188, L204) are not read aloud. The belief and its why_wrong are unchanged. Forks are listed as exact duplicates 'even if you make changes' (23:41), as in L147, though a modified fork is a near duplicate at repository level. '61,000' (25:49) rounds L155's 61,036. Decontamination is raised as 'arguably even more important' and not taught (26:58; see spoken_filtering and dedup-across-sources).

external_prerequisites.note: C4's cleaning pipeline (lecture 13) is where the 3-sentence-span exact dedup (L211-L213) belongs.

misconceptions.belief: For deduplication you want a cryptographic hash so that two different documents never collide.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The professor picks MurmurHash precisely because it is fast and not collision resistant (L185, L187); the collision rate of a 32/64-bit non-cryptographic hash is negligible for grouping, and speed is the binding constraint on huge R (L170).

misconceptions.belief: Exact-match dedup removes repeated boilerplate such as licenses and templated product pages.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Those are near duplicates that differ by a few tokens (L148, L151-L153); exact hashing has 'high precision' but 'does not deduplicate near duplicates' (L206-L207). The 61,036-times product description (L155) is the other case: Lee et al. 2021 report a 61-word span repeated verbatim inside otherwise different pages, which exact substring matching finds and whole-document exact hashing does not.

5: only the two identical 'hello' strings collapse.
6: hashing with a seed makes every string distinct.

predict.why: Exact match means identical strings (L194); 'Hello!' and 'hello there' are different strings with different hashes, so only the duplicate 'hello' is removed (L198-L204).
predict.targets_misconception: Exact-match dedup removes repeated boilerplate such as licenses and templated product pages.
predict.distractor_from: Option 1 from expecting fuzzy matching; option 3 from misunderstanding hashing as randomizing.

transfer.q: You want to remove the MIT license text that appears, with small formatting differences, at the top of millions of code files, without deleting the files. Fill in the three design-space choices (item, match, action) the lecture's framework asks for, and say which of the three choices rules out exact hashing even if you hashed the license paragraph instead of the whole file.
transfer.answer: Item: a paragraph or span (the license block), not the whole file. Match: near-duplicate (fraction of common sub-items), because formatting differs. Action: remove all but one occurrence (or remove all, since it is boilerplate), keeping the rest of each file. Exact hashing fails on the match choice: whole files differ, and even hashed paragraph by paragraph the license blocks differ by formatting, so exact match finds nothing (L148, L151, L207).
transfer.why: The three choices are independent (L164-L166); the lecture's own near-duplicate examples are licenses and copy/paste formatting differences (L151-L153).
transfer.varies: functional: the goal is removing a sub-item inside documents rather than removing whole documents
transfer.invariant: a dedup scheme is fully specified by item, match and action

check.q: C4 deduplicates exact 3-sentence spans. A store's product pages repeat the same three sentences of boilerplate, except that each page inserts its own product name into the second sentence. Which part of the dedup design space stops these spans from being removed?
choices: the hash: MurmurHash is not collision resistant enough
the item: 3-sentence spans are far too long ever to repeat
the action: C4 keeps one copy of every repeated span
the match: exact hashing misses spans differing by a name

check.why: L206-L214: exact dedup has high precision but does not deduplicate near duplicates. Spans that differ by one product name get different hashes, so nothing groups. A non-cryptographic hash only risks false merges, never missed ones (L183-L185).

'the action: C4 keeps one copy of every repeated span' <- plausible: confuses the action choice with whether a match was found

prompts.self_explain: Why is 'written in a MapReduce way' the property that lets this trivial-looking code scale to trillions of tokens?

presentations.notice: Only byte-identical items share a hash and so a group: a changed capital letter or a trailing period gives a different hash, and both lines are kept.

knowledge_points.label: Jaccard(A, B) = |A ∩ B| / |A ∪ B|; near duplicate ⇔ Jaccard ≥ threshold
knowledge_points.statement: Two documents, viewed as sets of items, have Jaccard similarity |A ∩ B| / |A ∪ B|; the professor's A = {1,2,3,4} and B = {1,2,3,5} share 3 of 5 distinct items, so Jaccard = 0.6, and two documents are near duplicates when their Jaccard similarity is at least a chosen threshold.

anchors.quote: Definition: Jaccard(A, B) = |A intersect B| / |A union B| ... A = {"1", "2", "3", "4"} ... B = {"1", "2", "3", "5"} ... intersection = len(A & B) ... union = len(A | B) ... return intersection / union
Definition: two documents are **near duplicates** if their Jaccard similarity >= threshold ... Algorithmic challenge: find near duplicates in linear time

we're going to define this called Jaccard similarity, which is a fairly standard notion. ... And Jaccard of two sets is basically the size of the intersection over the size of the union. ... and you divide, and Jaccard is 0.6.
0 means that they're disjoint, 1 means that they're identical. ... And we're going to say that two documents are near duplicates if their Jaccard similarity is above some threshold, let's say 0.99.

provenance.filtering_note: Evaluating the professor's code gives intersection = 3, union = 5, jaccard = 0.6 (plain Python, L226-L230). The professor does not say what the items of a real document are (shingles / n-grams); that is left to the MMDS chapter linked at L269. 'Approximate set membership' (L218) is his framing sentence, not a definition. Spoken evidence (32:18): the example threshold aloud is 0.99 (the code gives none); 'Jaccard is 0.6' is read off the @inspect (32:00). The items of a real document (shingles) are still not named aloud.

prerequisites.note: Jaccard is introduced as the 'similarity measure' needed once exact match is shown to miss near duplicates (L207, L219).

misconceptions.belief: Jaccard similarity is the fraction of A's items that also appear in B.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The denominator is the union, not |A| (L222): for A = {1,2,3,4}, B = {1,2,3,5}, 3/|A| would give 0.75, but Jaccard is 3/5 = 0.6. Jaccard is symmetric; the containment fraction is not.

misconceptions.belief: Two documents with Jaccard 0.6 are 60% identical in text.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Jaccard is over sets of items with multiplicity and order discarded (L222-L224); it measures overlap of distinct items, not character or token agreement.

predict.q: A = {1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8} and B = {1,2,3,4}. Without computing, is Jaccard(A, B) above, equal to, or below the professor's 0.6 example, and why?
choices: Above: B is entirely contained in A.
Equal: both share 4 items.
Below: the union is 8 and the intersection 4, so 0.5.
predict.answer: Below: the union is 8 and the intersection 4, so 0.5.
predict.why: Jaccard divides by the union (L222); full containment of a small set in a large one still gives a modest ratio because the union is the larger set.
predict.targets_misconception: Jaccard similarity is the fraction of A's items that also appear in B.
predict.distractor_from: Option 1 from the containment-fraction misconception; option 2 from counting the intersection alone.

transfer.q: Two web pages are shingled into 5-word sets: page P has 1,000 shingles, page Q has 1,000, and 900 are shared, so Jaccard(P, Q) ≈ 0.818. A third page Q' is Q with one extra paragraph adding 200 new shingles. What is Jaccard(P, Q'), to three decimals?
transfer.why: Jaccard(P, Q) = 900 / 1100 ≈ 0.818; Jaccard(P, Q') = 900 / 1300 ≈ 0.692. Appending unshared content lowered similarity because it grows the union without touching the intersection. |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B| (L222, L228); new unshared shingles enter only the denominator.
transfer.varies: functional: real shingle counts instead of the toy 4-element sets, and one set is extended

How does the professor define 'near duplicates'?

knowledge_points.label: MinHash: Pr[h(A) = h(B)] = Jaccard(A, B) via the random-permutation argument
knowledge_points.statement: MinHash of a set is the minimum of a seeded hash over its items; because a random hash induces a random permutation of all items and each item is equally likely to be first, the min of A equals the min of B exactly when the first item in A ∪ B lies in A ∩ B, so Pr[minhash(A) = minhash(B)] = |A ∩ B| / |A ∪ B| = Jaccard(A, B), which the lecture verifies with 100 seeds on the 0.6 example.

anchors.quote: MinHash: a random hash function h so that Pr[h(A) = h(B)] = Jaccard(A, B) ... Normally, you want different items to hash to different hashes ... but here, you want collision probability to depend on similarity ... return min(mmh3.hash(x, seed) for x in S)

Random hash function induces a permutation over items ... Look at which item is first in A and which item is first in B. ... Each item has the same probability as being first (min) ... If 1, 2, 3 is first, then first in A = first in B. ... If 4, 5 is first, then first in A ≠ first in B.

n = 100  # Generate this many random hash functions ... matches = [minhash(A, seed) == minhash(B, seed) for seed in range(n)] ... assert abs(estimated_jaccard - jaccard) < 0.01 ... Now we can hash our items, but a collision doesn't tell us Jaccard(A, B) > threshold.

normally, you want hash functions to define hash functions so that everything is hashing-- distinct elements are hashing to different things. ... But here you actually want collisions ... So similar things you want to collide more than disparate things.
Why are you taking the min? ... You can take the max, too. ... It doesn't really matter. ... It's just a way to break ties.

what the random hash function is doing is that it induces a permutation over the items. ... And then you look at which item is first, according to this permutation in A, and which item is first in B. ... So each item has the same probability of being first.
So I'm going to generate 100 different hash functions. ... and you get 0.6. ... And the key thing with the MinHash is that I don't have to do the n-squared thing.

provenance.filtering_note: estimated_jaccard (L262) depends on mmh3 seeds and is not restated; the assert at L263 guarantees it lies within 0.01 of 0.6, i.e. 59, 60 or 61 of the 100 seeds collide. The characteristic-matrix table (L246-L251) is the permutation argument's visual: rows 1-3 are in both columns, rows 4-5 in one. The professor does not discuss that the argument assumes no hash ties or that a real hash is only approximately a random permutation. Spoken evidence: the min is arbitrary, 'You can take the max, too. It doesn't really matter' (34:12-34:16), since any fixed rule for picking the first item under the induced permutation works; the code check is read aloud as 'you get 0.6' (36:47), consistent with L263's assert (this thread still states only 'within 0.01'); the payoff is said: compute each set's MinHash once and look for collisions, with no n-squared comparison (36:56-37:05). Hash ties are still not discussed.

prerequisites.note: The collision probability equals the Jaccard just computed (L237, L263).
Reuses mmh3 with a seed (L243); contrasts with the usual goal of distinct items hashing apart (L239-L240).

misconceptions.belief: MinHash is a better hash function that makes similar documents collide more often; it is still trying to avoid collisions for different documents.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The professor flips the goal: 'Normally, you want different items to hash to different hashes ... but here, you want collision probability to depend on similarity' (L239-L240); the design target is Pr[collision] = Jaccard exactly, not low collisions.

misconceptions.belief: One MinHash collision means the documents are near duplicates.
misconceptions.why_wrong: A single collision is a coin flip with probability Jaccard (L272); documents with Jaccard 0.3 collide 30% of the time. 'A collision doesn't tell us Jaccard(A, B) > threshold' (L265); that needs many hashes and banding.

predict.q: Sets A = {a, b, c, d, e, f} and B = {a, b, c, g, h, i} (Jaccard = 3/9). Using one seeded MinHash, what is the probability their minhashes are equal?
choices: 1/2: half of A's six items also appear in B.
1/3: the union's first item must be one of the 3 shared of 9.
Near 0: a good hash rarely collides on two different sets.
Near 1: MinHash is built so that similar sets always collide.
predict.answer: 1/3: the union's first item must be one of the 3 shared of 9.
predict.why: 1/3: the first item of the union under the random permutation must be one of the 3 shared items out of 9. Each of the 9 union items is equally likely to be first (L255); the mins agree iff that item is in both sets (L256-L257), which is 3 of 9 = Jaccard.
predict.targets_misconception: MinHash is a better hash function that makes similar documents collide more often; it is still trying to avoid collisions for different documents.
distractor_from: 'Near 0' <- misconception: 'MinHash is a better hash function ... still trying to avoid collisions for different documents.'
'Near 1' <- misconception: 'One MinHash collision means the documents are near duplicates.' (and the 'better hash for similar documents' half of the first)
'1/2' <- jaccard-similarity misconception: containment fraction mistaken for Jaccard

transfer.q: An engineer implements minhash(S, seed) as max(mmh3.hash(x, seed) for x in S) instead of min. Does Pr[h(A) = h(B)] still equal Jaccard(A, B)? Explain using the permutation argument, then say what breaks if instead they hash the whole set as one string.
transfer.answer: Yes: a random permutation read backwards is still a random permutation, so the max agrees iff the last item of A ∪ B lies in A ∩ B, again with probability |A ∩ B| / |A ∪ B|. Hashing the whole set as one string destroys the property: any single differing item changes the hash, so Pr[collision] is near 0 for every pair with Jaccard < 1, back to exact-match dedup.
transfer.why: The argument needs only that one uniformly random item of the union decides the value (L253-L257); min and max both do that, a whole-set hash does not.
transfer.varies: functional: the aggregation (min vs max) and the hashing granularity (item vs whole set) change
transfer.invariant: collision iff a uniformly random element of the union is shared

check.q: Shingle sets A (9 items) and B (7 items) share 5 items. You compute minhash(A, seed) and minhash(B, seed) for 200 independent seeds. How many seeds do you expect to give equal minhashes?
check.why: |A ∩ B| = 5 and |A ∪ B| = 9 + 7 - 5 = 11, so each seed collides with probability Jaccard = 5/11 ≈ 0.455 (the first item of the union under the random permutation must be a shared one). Expected matches: 200 x 5/11 ≈ 90.9.
check.varies: new set sizes and many seeds instead of max-vs-min or whole-set hashing
check.targets_misconception: One MinHash collision means the documents are near duplicates.

retrieval.q: State the defining property of a MinHash function.
retrieval.answer: Pr[h(A) = h(B)] = Jaccard(A, B).

retrieval.q: In the permutation argument, when do the first items of A and B coincide?
retrieval.answer: When the first item of the union under the permutation is in both sets (items 1, 2, 3); if 4 or 5 is first they differ.

retrieval.q: The lecture estimates Jaccard({1,2,3,4}, {1,2,3,5}) from 100 MinHash seeds and asserts a tolerance on the result. How close to the true Jaccard must the estimate be?

knowledge_points.label: LSH banding: P(collide) = 1 − (1 − s^r)^b; r shifts right/sharpens, b shifts left
knowledge_points.statement: To turn 'collision probability equals similarity' into 'collide iff similarity > threshold', use n = b · r MinHashes split into b bands of r rows; A and B collide if some band has all r hashes equal, so with Jaccard s the probability is 1 − (1 − s^r)^b, an S-curve whose and-or structure sharpens the threshold: raising r moves it right and steepens it (harder to match), raising b moves it left (easier), and the professor's example s = 0.8, b = 5, r = 10 evaluates to about 0.43.

anchors.quote: Suppose we hash examples with just one MinHash function ... P[A and B collide] = Jaccard(A, B) ... On average, more similar items will collide, but very stochastic... ... Goal: have A and B collide if Jaccard(A, B) > threshold ... Solution: use n hash functions ... Break up into b bands of r hash functions each (n = b * r)

n = 12      # Number of hash functions ... b = 3       # Number of bands ... r = 4       # Number of hash functions per band ... h1 h2 h3 h4  |  h5 h6 h7 h8  |  h9 h10 h11 h12 ... Key: A and B collide if for *some* band, *all* its hash functions return same value ... the and-or structure of the bands sharpens the threshold

prob_match = sim ** r                        # Probability that a fixed band matches ... prob_collision = 1 - (1 - prob_match) ** b   # Probability that some band matches ... prob_collision = get_prob_collision(sim=0.8, b=5, r=10)

sims = [0.7, 0.75, 0.8, 0.85, 0.9, 0.95, 0.98] ... probs = {sim: get_prob_collision(sim=sim, b=10, r=10) for sim in sims} ... Increasing r sharpens the threshold and moves the curve to the right (harder to match) ... Increasing b moves the curve to the left (easier to match)

anchors.quote: So now we can hash our items, but we're not done yet because a collision doesn't tell us the Jaccard is above some threshold, which is what we want. ... It's stochastic, and I can't really get anything reliable here.
So the solution is to use more hash functions. ... And these hash functions are going to be independent.

We say that A and B collide if for some band all of its hash functions return the same value. ... But you don't have to have all the hash functions return the same value. ... So there's this and-or structure here that is doing the lifting here.

So that's 0.8 to the r. ... So the probability of a fixed band matching is generally quite low. ... So the probability of collision is 0.4. ... And you're expected to be higher because you're given B tries to get a match.
So when you increase r, the threshold sharpens and moves the curve to the right. ... So before it was 0.25, and now it's 0.008.

And then increasing b has the effect of moving the curve to the left. ... So now we're making-- before this, 0.9 was only 0.72, and now it's 0.92. ... But of course, if you can increase b and r too much, then it can be more expensive.

prerequisites.note: A band matches with probability s^r because each of its r MinHashes collides independently with probability s (L293).

misconceptions.belief: More hash functions always make LSH stricter.
misconceptions.why_wrong: It depends on how they are arranged: adding rows per band (r) is an AND and makes matching harder, adding bands (b) is an OR and makes it easier (L287, L305, L308). Going from b = 10, r = 20 to b = 20, r = 20 doubles n yet raises P(collide) at s = 0.85 from 0.33 to 0.55 (evaluated from L306, L309).

misconceptions.belief: With b bands of r rows, two documents collide only if all n = b · r hashes agree.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Collision requires all r hashes to agree in *some* band, not all n (L287); requiring all n would be s^n, a curve far to the right with no OR to pull it back.

predict.q: At s = 0.8, the professor's b = 5, r = 10 gives P(collide) ≈ 0.43. Keeping r = 10, you raise b to 20. Before computing, which way does P(collide) at s = 0.8 move, and roughly where does it land?

Up, to about 0.9: more bands is an OR over more chances to match.
Unchanged: the threshold depends only on r.

transfer.q: A team has n = 100 MinHashes and considers (b = 20, r = 5) versus (b = 5, r = 20); they want to reject pairs with s ≤ 0.6. Decide first which layout is more permissive and why, then type only P(collide) at s = 0.6 for the (b = 20, r = 5) layout, as a decimal.
transfer.why: (b = 20, r = 5) is more permissive: fewer rows per band (weaker AND) and more bands (stronger OR). At s = 0.6: 1 − (1 − 0.6^5)^20 = 1 − (1 − 0.0778)^20 ≈ 0.80, so most 0.6-pairs would wrongly collide; (b = 5, r = 20): 1 − (1 − 0.6^20)^5 ≈ 1.8e-4, essentially none. At s = 0.9 the second layout still gives 1 − (1 − 0.1216)^5 ≈ 0.48, so with n = 100 the stricter layout rejects well but catches only about half of the true near duplicates; more bands at r = 20 would be needed. Same n, different split: r sets where the S-curve rises, b sets how fast it saturates (L293-L294, L305, L308).
transfer.varies: functional: fixed total n, the b/r split is the variable; the lecture varied b and r separately
