retrieval.answer: A and B collide if for some band all of its r hash functions return the same value.

retrieval.q: Which way does the S-curve move when r increases, and when b increases?
retrieval.answer: Increasing r moves it right and sharpens it (harder to match); increasing b moves it left (easier to match).

prompts.self_explain: Why does an AND inside bands followed by an OR across bands produce an S-shape, when either operation alone would not?

presentations.notice: Each band is an AND (its bar is s^r, and it shrinks when r grows); the pair collides on an OR over the b bars. More bands means more chances, so the curve moves left; more rows per band shrinks every chance, so it moves right and steepens.
listen for: raising r moves the S-curve right (0.25 to 0.008), raising b moves it left (0.72 to 0.92 at s = 0.9), and both cost hashes

knowledge_points.label: LSH threshold ≈ (1/b)^(1/r); at it, one band matches in expectation and P ≈ 1 − 1/e
knowledge_points.statement: The S-curve's phase transition sits at s* = (1/b)^(1/r), the similarity at which a fixed band matches with probability s*^r = 1/b so exactly one of the b bands is expected to match, giving P(collide) = 1 − (1 − 1/b)^b ≈ 1 − 1/e ≈ 0.63; for the Lee et al. setting n = 9000, b = 20, r = 450 the threshold evaluates to 0.9934, so only documents sharing over 99% of their shingles reliably collide.

anchors.quote: Example setting ... : n = 9000, b = 20, r = 450 ... What is the threshold (where the phase transition happens)? ... threshold = (1 / b) ** (1 / r)
Probability that a fixed band matches: ... prob_match = (1 / b) ... Probability that A and B collide is a constant (≈ 1-1/e): ... prob_collision = 1 - (1 - 1 / b) ** b

anchors.ref: paper linked at L312 (n = 9000, b = 20, r = 450)

anchors.quote: So let's look at a more real-world setting. ... So in this paper on deduplication, they had b, 20 bands, and r is 450.

And in general, the phase transition happens at a threshold, which is 1/b b raised to the power of 1/r. ... So if you want to filter based on Jaccard greater than 0.9, then you basically have to set b and r such that this is 0.9.

So remember the probability of the fixed band matches is 1/b. ... So the probability of collision is 0.64. ... everything below it should go to 0, as b and r increases, and everything above, it should go to 1 as b and r increases.
So this method is called MinHash LSH because LSH really works for any hash functions.

provenance.filtering_note: Evaluating the professor's formulas gives threshold = (1/20)^(1/450) = 0.99336 (L316), prob_match = 0.05 (L319) and prob_collision = 1 − 0.95^20 = 0.6415 (L321), versus 1 − 1/e = 0.6321; the professor writes '≈ 1-1/e' and the approximation improves as b grows. The n = 9000, b = 20, r = 450 configuration is Lee et al.'s as read by the professor (L312); the lecture does not say why they chose such a high threshold. The professor does not derive (1/b)^(1/r) from the curve's inflection; it is the point where s^r = 1/b, and he presents it as 'where the phase transition happens' (L315). Spoken evidence (47:10-47:22): how the formula is used: pick b and r so that (1/b)^(1/r) equals the target Jaccard ('0.9' in his example), then change b and r together to sharpen the transition. '0.64' is read aloud (47:47), matching L321's 0.6415, and he explains it as the centre of the transition, with everything below going to 0 and everything above to 1 as b and r grow. He still does not say why Lee et al. chose such a high threshold. The general method is named 'MinHash LSH' (48:14).

prerequisites.note: The threshold is read off the same 1 − (1 − s^r)^b curve (L294) by setting s^r = 1/b.

misconceptions.belief: At the LSH threshold, documents collide with probability about 1/2.
misconceptions.why_wrong: At s* the expected number of matching bands is 1, and P(at least one) = 1 − (1 − 1/b)^b ≈ 1 − 1/e ≈ 0.63 (L320-L321), 0.6415 for b = 20.

misconceptions.belief: A dedup setting with 9000 hash functions must be catching loosely similar documents.
misconceptions.why_wrong: With b = 20, r = 450 the threshold is (1/20)^(1/450) ≈ 0.993 (evaluated from L316): the heavy r makes matching very hard, so only near-identical documents collide. The count n alone says nothing; the b/r split does.

predict.q: Lee et al.'s b = 20, r = 450 gives a threshold near 0.993. A team keeps n = 9000 but regroups it as b = 90, r = 100. Before computing, does the threshold move up or down, and to roughly what value?
choices: Up, nearer 1: more bands means more agreement is required.
Down, to about 0.956: fewer rows per band lowers the exponent, (1/90)^(1/100) ≈ 0.956.
Unchanged: the threshold depends only on n.
predict.answer: Down, to about 0.956: fewer rows per band lowers the exponent, (1/90)^(1/100) ≈ 0.956.
predict.why: s* = (1/b)^(1/r) (L316); r falls from 450 to 100, which dominates the modest rise in b. Evaluating: exp(ln(1/90)/100) = exp(−0.045) ≈ 0.956.
predict.targets_misconception: A dedup setting with 9000 hash functions must be catching loosely similar documents.
predict.distractor_from: Option 1 from confusing more bands with stricter matching (the lsh-band-sharpening misconception); option 3 from the 'n alone decides' misconception.

transfer.q: You want LSH to treat documents as near duplicates at Jaccard about 0.8 and can afford r = 10 rows per band. Using the threshold approximation s* ≈ (1/b)^(1/r), how many bands b does that require (one decimal)?
transfer.why: b must satisfy (1/b)^(1/10) = 0.8, i.e. b = 0.8^−10 ≈ 9.3, so about 9 or 10 bands (n ≈ 90-100). At the threshold P(collide) = 1 − (1 − 1/b)^b ≈ 0.65 for b = 9 (0.63 in the large-b limit), not 1: a pair exactly at 0.8 is still missed about a third of the time. Invert s* = (1/b)^(1/r) for b (L316); the collision probability at s* is the constant 1 − (1 − 1/b)^b (L321).
transfer.varies: functional: the threshold is the given and b the unknown, reversing the lecture's computation
transfer.invariant: s*^r = 1/b, one expected matching band at threshold

retrieval.q: Write the formula for the LSH threshold in terms of b and r.
At the threshold, what is the probability that a fixed band matches, and approximately what is the overall collision probability?
retrieval.answer: 1/b for a fixed band; overall 1 − (1 − 1/b)^b ≈ 1 − 1/e ≈ 0.63.

retrieval.q: What n, b, r does the professor quote from Lee et al. 2021?

prompts.self_explain: Why does the collision probability at the threshold converge to the same constant 1 − 1/e no matter how b and r are chosen?

presentations.notice: Put s on the dashed s* line: whatever b and r are, each band's AND bar is then exactly 1/b long and the OR bar reads about 0.63. Regrouping the same n into more, shorter bands moves s* down.
listen for: set (1/b)^(1/r) to the target Jaccard; at the threshold P(collide) is about 0.64

knowledge_points.label: Deduplicate over the whole mixture, not only inside each source
knowledge_points.statement: Deduplication compares items only within the collection it is run on, so deduplicating each dataset separately cannot remove a document that sits in two datasets (a page in both a Common Crawl extract and a curated web set, the same repository in two code dumps); because sources are often redundant, dedup has to be run over the union of all sources, a step the professor says is sometimes skipped but should not be.

anchors.quote: And sometimes the deduplication will happen within a data set. ... But you actually have to do deduplication across your entire data set because often data sets can be redundant. ... So sometimes that's not done, but it should be.
Related to deduplication is also decontamination, which is arguably even more important, too. ... And it's the same deal, is that you want to make sure that your test set is not in your training set.

provenance.filtering_note: Spoken only (48:55-49:14). deduplication() (L145-L175) defines the design space and the algorithms on one collection of items and never says over which collection dedup runs; aloud, the last remark of the section is that dedup 'will happen within a data set' but must be done 'across your entire data set because often data sets can be redundant. So sometimes that's not done, but it should be.' The examples of overlapping sources (a curated set filtered from Common Crawl, Wikipedia inside Common Crawl) are this thread's; the professor names none. The far transfer uses the decontamination aside (26:58-27:14: 'the same deal ... your test set is not in your training set'), which the lecture does not develop; treating decontamination as cross-collection dedup is this thread's framing. Placed after lsh-threshold-one-over-b, where it is said.

prerequisites.note: The design space (item, match, action) and the hash-groupby procedure whose scope this KP is about.
Said right after the LSH section; near-duplicate detection has the same scope question.

misconceptions.belief: If every source in the mixture has been deduplicated, the mixture is deduplicated.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Dedup only compares items inside the collection it runs on, so a copy in source A is never compared with a copy in source B; 'you actually have to do deduplication across your entire data set' (49:08).

misconceptions.belief: Cross-source duplicates are rare, because each dataset is collected independently.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Datasets are often built from the same crawls and mirrors ('often data sets can be redundant', 49:08); a curated web set filtered from Common Crawl overlaps Common Crawl by construction.

predict.q: A team mixes three sources: a Common Crawl extract, a Wikipedia dump, and a 'high-quality web' set that was itself filtered out of Common Crawl. Each source was MinHash-deduplicated on its own before mixing. Which documents can still appear more than once in the mixture?
choices: Pages held by two or more of the sources
None: every source has already been deduplicated
Only near duplicates that MinHash missed
Only pages repeated inside a single source
predict.answer: Pages held by two or more of the sources
predict.why: Each dedup run compared items only within its own source, so a page in both the Common Crawl extract and the filtered web set (or a Wikipedia article copied onto a crawled page) was never compared with its twin. Dedup has to run 'across your entire data set because often data sets can be redundant' (49:08).
predict.targets_misconception: If every source in the mixture has been deduplicated, the mixture is deduplicated.
distractor_from: 'None: every source has already been deduplicated' <- misconception: per-source dedup is taken to cover the mixture
'Only near duplicates that MinHash missed' <- plausible: blames the algorithm's recall instead of its scope
'Only pages repeated inside a single source' <- inverts the scope: those are exactly what per-source dedup removes

transfer.q: Before training, you deduplicate each training source internally, and you separately confirm that a benchmark's test set has no duplicates inside it. Is the test set now guaranteed to be absent from the training data? Say what comparison is missing and how it relates to the dedup scope.
transfer.answer: No. Neither check ever compares a test item with a training item. Decontamination is a dedup run over the union of the training mixture and the test set (matching test items against training items and removing the training copies); internal dedup of each collection says nothing about overlaps between collections.
transfer.why: The professor calls decontamination 'the same deal ... make sure that your test set is not in your training set' (27:04) and says dedup must cover the entire dataset (49:08). Whatever collection a dedup run is given is the only place it can find copies.
transfer.varies: the second collection is a held-out test set instead of another training source, and the goal is removal for evaluation validity rather than for compute
transfer.invariant: dedup finds copies only within the collection it is run on; overlap between collections needs a run over their union

check.q: Three sources are each free of internal duplicates: A has 2,000 documents, B has 800 and C has 500. Exactly 300 of B's documents also appear in A, and 100 of C's documents also appear in B but not in A. No other document appears in more than one source. After deduplicating over the union of A, B and C, keeping one copy of each document, how many documents remain? Type only the number.
check.why: The union holds 2,000 + 800 + 500 = 3,300 documents with 300 + 100 = 400 extra copies, so 3,300 - 400 = 2,900 remain. Per-source dedup would have left all 3,300, because every source was already internally unique.
check.targets_misconception: If every source in the mixture has been deduplicated, the mixture is deduplicated.
check.varies: surface: count the documents left by dedup over the union instead of naming which documents survive per-source dedup
check.invariant: copies shared between sources are removed only by a dedup run over the union

retrieval.q: Over which collection does the professor say deduplication must be run, and why?
retrieval.answer: Over the entire dataset (the union of all sources), not just within each source, because datasets are often redundant.

retrieval.q: Which related step does the professor call 'arguably even more important' than deduplication, and what does it check?
retrieval.answer: Decontamination: making sure the test set is not in the training set.

prompts.self_explain: Why can a pipeline in which every source passed MinHash-LSH dedup still train on the same document twice, and what single change fixes it?

presentations.notice: With the scope set to 'within each source', identical lines held by two sources are never compared and both copies are kept; only the union scope removes them.
listen for: 'you actually have to do deduplication across your entire data set because often data sets can be redundant'

knowledge_points.label: Mixing baselines (vibes, uniform, proportional) and the epoching trap: 50 epochs on a 10B source
knowledge_points.statement: A data mixture is a distribution p(s) over sources; the baselines are vibes, uniform (p ∝ 1) and proportional (p ∝ num_tokens(s)); upweighting a high-quality source is limited by diversity and by finiteness, because training for N tokens draws p(s)·N tokens from source s, so a 50/50 mix of a 10T and a 10B source trained for 1T tokens makes 0.05 epochs of the first and 50 epochs of the second, and UniMax fixes this with a hard cap p(s)·N ≤ C on every source.

anchors.quote: Key question: what distribution over the data sources should we use? ... Baselines: ... Vibes: set p(s) manually based on intuition (quite common) ... Uniform sampling: sample uniformly (p(s) ∝ 1) ... Proportional mixing: sample proportional to the number of tokens in a source (p(s) ∝ num_tokens(s))

Intuition: should upweight higher quality sources ... We want to ensure diversity (e.g., across incomparable sources: literature, code, papers) ... Each source is finite, so if put too much weight on a small source, then need to epoch over it

"low": trillion(10),  # 10T tokens (abundant) ... "high": billion(10),  # 10B tokens (scarce) ... p = {"low": 0.5, "high": 0.5}  # Naive data mixture ... train_tokens = trillion(1) ... high_num_epochs = (p["high"] * train_tokens) / source_token_counts["high"] ... 50x epochs on high quality data...can lead to overfitting!

Setting: balancing different languages for multilingual models ... Previous work: between uniform and proportional mixing (p(s) ∝ num_tokens(s)^α for α in [0, 1]) ... Idea: sample sources uniformly but with a hard **cap** C on number of epochs for any source ... Specifically, p(s) * num_training_tokens ≤ C for all sources s

anchors.ref: paper linked at L337; composition figure shown at L338

anchors.quote: But language models are trained on multiple data sources. ... There's Nemotron, there's FinePDFs, which we talked about.
Vibes, which is, I guess, the opposite of first principle, is you just manually set it based on some intuition, which is more often than you might think, what people do.
But you might worry that if you have a huge, low-quality data set, that's going to eat up a lot of your token.

One is that you do want to ensure some diversity. ... You can't really say that this paper is higher quality than this code because they're just incomparable objects, maybe. ... So if you put too much weight on a small source, then you essentially run out of that source

So this is less than 1. ... So basically, that means 5% of the tokens in this low-quality data set, I'm going to touch and train on once. ... And then if you look at high quality, you'll see that the number of epochs is 50
So this is actually really important. ... And some big model runs have messed this up.

And I guess the point is that you don't need 50 epochs. ... Sorry, best case is wasting compute, and worst case, you're overfitting. ... So this is basically-- the lesson is look at how many epochs you're actually doing on your data.
So the question is, when you train, how do the mixtures get realized? ... Usually, every sequence comes from one mixture component. ... You're not sampling per token.

before some works would essentially take the proportional mixing and raise it to some power to flatten it out the distribution. ... Let's sample the sources uniformly, but with a hard cap on the number of epochs. ... Here, you say I'm only going to take 20 epochs over a particular data source.

provenance.filtering_note: Evaluating the professor's arithmetic gives low_num_epochs = 0.5 × 1e12 / 1e13 = 0.05 and high_num_epochs = 0.5 × 1e12 / 1e10 = 50 (L363-L364). The Marin token viewer screenshot (L335) and the Pile composition figure (L338) are shown; their per-source counts are not restated. The example mixture p = {Wikipedia 0.3, CC 0.5, GitHub 0.2} (L343) is notation only. UniMax's cap is written as p(s) · num_training_tokens ≤ C (L371), which reads as a token cap; the professor's gloss is 'cap C on number of epochs' (L370), i.e. C is in units of the source size. The lecture does not say how many epochs is too many. Spoken evidence: the epoch arithmetic is read aloud as '5% of the tokens in this low-quality data set, I'm going to touch and train on once' and 'the number of epochs is 50' (54:54-55:30); why proportional mixing is not enough: a huge low-quality source 'is going to eat up a lot of your token' (52:25); vibes are 'more often than you might think, what people do' (51:25); 'some big model runs have messed this up' (55:39, unnamed). Partial answer to 'The lecture does not say how many epochs is too many': 50 epochs is 'best case ... wasting compute, and worst case, you're overfitting' (56:43-56:46), and the UniMax cap is illustrated with 'I'm only going to take 20 epochs' (59:21), an example value, not UniMax's setting and not a rule. The cap is read aloud as p(s) times training tokens 'less than or equal to the cap' (59:40), with the same unit ambiguity as L371. Q&A (57:26-58:16): a mixture is realized per sequence, each sequence drawn from one component, so each batch is mixed and nothing is sampled per token. Q&A (1:12:07-1:12:50): mixture components need not be given sources; Common Crawl can be split by topic and by quality into a two-dimensional grid of cells (attributed to the Nemotron paper and a 'web organizer'; captions 'IT folks', presumably AI2's WebOrganizer). UniMax's 'simple procedure' for meeting the cap is not described (59:51).

external_prerequisites.note: The Pile's 22 hand-weighted subsets (imported at L7, shown at L337-L338) are the 'vibes' baseline in practice.

misconceptions.belief: Mixture weights are just sampling proportions; a 50/50 mix treats both sources equally.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Weights are per-token draw probabilities over a fixed budget, so the number of passes over each source is p(s)·N / num_tokens(s) (L363-L364): 50/50 over 1T tokens is 0.05 epochs of a 10T source and 50 epochs of a 10B source, 'can lead to overfitting' (L365).

misconceptions.belief: Upweighting the highest-quality source is always the right move.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Two limits (L352-L353): diversity across incomparable sources (code, papers, literature) and finiteness, which forces repeated epochs over a small source. UniMax caps epochs for exactly this reason (L370-L371).

predict.q: A mixture gives weight 0.3 to a 30B-token curated source and trains for 2T tokens. Decide first whether the curated source will be seen fewer than once, a few times, or many times; then type only the epoch count.
predict.why: Many times: 0.3 × 2e12 / 3e10 = 20 epochs. epochs = p(s) × train_tokens / num_tokens(s) (L363-L364); a modest weight on a small source over a long run still multiplies into many passes.
predict.targets_misconception: Mixture weights are just sampling proportions; a 50/50 mix treats both sources equally.

transfer.q: A multilingual run has 5 languages with 2T, 500B, 50B, 5B and 500M tokens and a 1T budget. Under uniform mixing (p = 0.2 each), how many epochs does the 500M-token language make?
transfer.why: The 500M-token language: uniform weight ignores finiteness. Epochs = 0.2 × 1e12 / 5e8 = 400. UniMax requires p(s) × 1e12 ≤ 4 × 5e8 = 2e9, so p(s) ≤ 0.002 for that language, with the freed mass redistributed to languages under their cap. Uniform is p ∝ 1 (L347); the epoch formula is L363-L364; UniMax's cap is p(s) × num_training_tokens ≤ C (L371) with C in epochs of the source (L370).
transfer.varies: domain: languages instead of quality tiers (UniMax's own setting), with five sources instead of two
transfer.invariant: epochs = p(s) × budget / source size; the cap bounds that product

retrieval.q: Name the three mixing baselines and the proportionality each uses.
retrieval.answer: Vibes (manual); uniform (p ∝ 1); proportional (p ∝ num_tokens(s)).

retrieval.q: A 50/50 mix of a 10T-token source and a 10B-token source is trained for 1T tokens. Give the epoch formula and the epochs of each source.
retrieval.answer: epochs(s) = p(s) × train_tokens / num_tokens(s): 0.5 × 1T / 10T = 0.05 epochs of the 10T source, 0.5 × 1T / 10B = 50 epochs of the 10B source.

retrieval.q: Prior multilingual work mixed sources somewhere between uniform and proportional. What form did it use, and what does UniMax do instead?
retrieval.answer: p(s) ∝ num_tokens(s)^α with α in [0, 1]. UniMax samples uniformly but with a hard cap on epochs for every source: p(s) × num_training_tokens ≤ C.

knowledge_points.label: Regression-based mixing, its two hopes, and simulated epoching (downsample by 0.01)
knowledge_points.statement: Regression-based mixing samples many mixtures (e.g. Dirichlet), trains small models, fits a regression from mixture to downstream target and optimizes it, which rests on two hopes, that the regression is accurate at its minimizer and that the optimal mixture transfers from small to large scale; the second fails when a small run's optimum (e.g. 0.9 on a 10B source) would epoch heavily at large scale, so simulated epoching downsamples every source by small_run_tokens / large_run_tokens (10B / 1T = 0.01, turning 10T → 100B and 10B → 100M) so that the small run epochs like the large one and its optimum shifts toward balance.

anchors.quote: Define distribution over mixtures `p` (e.g., Dirichlet) ... Define regression method (e.g., linear, gradient boosted trees) ... Define target based on downstream evals (careful not to overfit!) ... Discrepancy between small and large scale (tradeoff cost and accuracy) ... Hope 1: regression model is accurate at minimizer ... Hope 2: optimal data mixtures transfer from small to large scale

Hold on. There's at least one scale-dependent effect: ... If train small models on low token counts: ... p = {"low": 0.1, "high": 0.9}  # More mass on high quality data ... But if train large model on this mixture, we will epoch a ton on high quality data and overfit!

General idea: make small scale look like large scale (general theme of this course) ... Instantiation: downsample all sources proportionally ... ratio = small_run_tokens / large_run_tokens ... downsampled_source_token_counts = {s: count * ratio for s, count in source_token_counts.items()} ... In this downsampled mixture, models that epoch too much won't look good. ... So the optimum will be more balanced.
Regression-based mixing: estimate mixture → loss at small scale, optimize (analogous to scaling laws) ... Important consideration: epoching and overfitting (solution: cap or simulated)

anchors.ref: paper linked at L373; figure shown at L374
paper linked at L373; methods comparison figure shown at L379

anchors.quote: So first, let's say you're trying to train a large-scale model. ... So you go to a small scale, let's say 300 million parameters, and you try different data mixtures. ... It could be some downstream values. ... It could be perplexity, whatever you want.
Often this is based on downstream evals. ... You're going to upweight all the code data. ... So proportional mixing and uniform mixing don't have this problem because you're not looking.

And this is a cost and accuracy trade-off. ... But if you train large models to do this, well, there's no point in doing any of this. ... You're basically doing hyperparameter tuning at the largest scale, which is too expensive.

So the hope is that the minimizer, your optimal data mixture, that regression model is still accurate. ... But when you're optimizing, you're essentially trying to go to potentially the extremes where you might not have as much coverage.

And the other thing is that optimal data mixtures, you just hope that they transfer from small scale to large scale. ... at least at the scales that open community works with, it tends to be true or not plainly false. ... But clearly, there are scale-dependent effects.

So one way to fix this, which is done in this Olmix paper is you can just cap the number of epochs. ... But one name for it is simulated epoching. ... And the principle here is that make your small scale look like your large scale. ... We saw it when we talked about muP.
you don't get to just train on Wikipedia. ... So you're simulating the data scarcity that you would get in your high regime at low scale.
So the question is, if you're downsampling, is there a risk? ... But there might be rounding errors where you end up, instead of training once on this data set, you train like zero times by accident.

provenance.filtering_note: Evaluating the professor's arithmetic gives ratio = 1e10 / 1e12 = 0.01 (L397) and downsampled counts low = 1e11 (100B), high = 1e8 (100M) (L398). The mixtures p = {low 0.1, high 0.9} (L389) and p = {low 0.7, high 0.3} (L401) are illustrative values the professor types, not fitted optima; this thread adds that at 1T tokens the 0.9 mixture would mean 90 epochs of the 10B source and that 0.3 on the downsampled 100M source over a 10B run is 30 epochs, as evaluations of his epoch formula. The RegMix figure (L374) and the mixing-methods comparison (L379) are shown; their numbers are not restated. The lecture does not specify the regression target beyond 'downstream evals'. Correction (1:01:10-1:01:18): the note says the lecture does not specify the regression target beyond 'downstream evals'. Aloud: 'It could be some downstream values. It could be perplexity, whatever you want.' Olmix's epoch cap is named as an alternative fix (1:07:24); simulated epoching is tied to muP's 'make your small scale look like your large scale' (1:07:47-1:08:02). The 0.9 mixture is called 'a made-up example' (1:06:48). Same shape of argument: a small-run optimum (strict filter / heavy upweighting) does not transfer to a long run because the long run exhausts the small set.

misconceptions.why_wrong: That is Hope 2 (L381), and the professor immediately gives a counterexample (L383-L390): a small run on low token counts can afford 0.9 on a 10B source, but a 1T-token run with that weight makes 90 passes over it and overfits.

misconceptions.belief: Simulated epoching means running the small models for more epochs.
misconceptions.why_wrong: It downsamples the sources, not the run: every source is multiplied by small_run_tokens / large_run_tokens = 0.01 (L394, L397-L398), so the small run sees each source the same number of times the large run would.

predict.q: A small-scale regression study finds the best mixture puts 0.9 on a 10B-token curated source. The production run is 1T tokens. Decide first what goes wrong at scale; then type only the number of epochs of the curated source that the production run makes.
predict.why: The curated source is epoched heavily and the model overfits: 0.9 × 1e12 / 1e10 = 90 epochs. L389-L390: the small run never saw the finiteness of the 10B source, so its optimum violates Hope 2. Epochs = p × train_tokens / num_tokens (L363-L364).
predict.targets_misconception: The mixture that minimizes loss in cheap small-scale runs is the mixture to use at full scale.

transfer.q: Your pilot runs are 20B tokens and the production run is 4T tokens. Simulated epoching downsamples every source by the pilot/production ratio. What is that ratio, as a decimal?
transfer.why: ratio = 2e10 / 4e12 = 0.005; downsampled sizes 40B, 2B and 100M. A pilot with 0.5 on the smallest source draws 1e10 tokens from a 100M-token pool: 100 epochs, the same as production would make, so its loss degrades and the regression learns to put less weight there; the fitted optimum becomes more balanced. Downsample all sources by small_run_tokens / large_run_tokens (L394, L397-L398) so that epochs per source match across scales; 'models that epoch too much won't look good' (L399).
transfer.varies: functional: three sources and a different budget ratio; the pilot and production sizes are both new
transfer.invariant: proportional downsampling preserves epochs-per-source between the small and large run

retrieval.answer: Any two of: a distribution over mixtures (e.g. Dirichlet); a regression method (e.g. linear, gradient boosted trees); a target based on downstream evals.

retrieval.q: State the two hopes regression-based mixing rests on.
retrieval.answer: Hope 1: the regression is accurate at its minimizer. Hope 2: optimal mixtures transfer from small to large scale.

retrieval.q: Simulated epoching lets a 10B-token small run stand in for a 1T-token large run. What does it do to the sources, and by what factor?
retrieval.answer: Downsamples every source proportionally by small_run_tokens / large_run_tokens = 10B / 1T = 0.01 (10T → 100B, 10B → 100M), so the small run epochs like the large one.

knowledge_points.label: Post-training data recipe: environments, prompts, teacher responses; OpenThoughts' findings
knowledge_points.statement: Post-training data is built by defining environments, defining tasks or prompts, and collecting responses from a strong teacher model; OpenThoughts (as read by the professor) distilled 1.2M examples from QwQ-32B over prompts from 27 human and synthetic sources and found that sampling 16 responses per prompt helps, that a better model is not necessarily a better teacher (QwQ-32B beat DeepSeek-R1 as teacher), that answer filtering did not help, and that smaller high-quality prompt sources beat large diverse ones.

anchors.quote: Recipe: ... 1. Define a set of environments ... 2. Define a set of tasks / prompts ... 3. Collect responses from a strong model (teacher)

1.2M examples using QwQ-32B as a teacher ... Questions come from 27 human and synthetic sources (e.g., StackExchange, NuminaMath, Chemistry) ... Sampling multiple (16) responses per prompt is helpful ... Better models aren't necessarily better teachers: QwQ-32B is a better teacher than DeepSeek-R1 ... Answer filtering wasn't helpful ... Smaller high quality sources (e.g., OpenMath-2-Math) is better than large diverse sources
Post-training data: looks like evaluations, use of synthetic data
Generating prompts: fully-synthetic, semi-synthetic (real environment + synthetic tasks), real (GitHub PRs) ... Responses: from capable models (that are also good teachers)

anchors.ref: paper linked at L415; figures shown at L418 and L423

anchors.quote: So when you look at post-training, a lot of the data becomes very task-dependent. ... And I'm not going to do a comprehensive review.

So implicitly, at least in the open community, almost all the post-training data, most of it, is synthetically generated. ... You can also replace a strong model with a human, but that is slow and costs a lot of money.
It was motivated by when o1 came out ... And they eventually came out with 1.2 million examples using this teacher model.

They show that having a few sources was actually good than trying to do all sources. ... Sampling multiple generations is helpful, like 16. ... having better models aren't necessarily better teachers. ... They also found that basic answer filtering wasn't helpful.
So the 1.2 million is examples, but divided by 16 gives you the number of actual questions.

You can have fully synthetic. ... You can have semi-synthetic, where you have real environment and synthetic tasks, or you can have real. ... And the responses generally are coming from just capable models, but they also need to be good teachers.

knowledge_points.label: SWE data: synthetic bugs, real PRs, and trading execution feedback for scale
knowledge_points.statement: Software-engineering agent data varies along two axes, how tasks are made and whether trajectories get execution feedback: SWE-smith injects bugs with an LM (128 repos → 50K tasks); SWE-rebench mines real PRs and uses an LM to install dependencies and judge PR quality (450K PRs → 21K executable tasks from 3.4K repos); SWE-Zero drops repository-specific execution because strong models' internal 'world model' of code lets them solve many tasks without it (300K trajectories from 150K PRs, distilled from Qwen3-Coder-480B, versus SWE-Hero's 13K executing trajectories), scaling to 12M trajectories, at the cost of needing filters and guards such as removing future git commits to prevent 'git hacking'.

anchors.quote: Given a repository, use LM to generate tasks (introduce bugs with LM) ... 128 GitHub repositories yields 50K tasks

SWE tasks have heavy dependencies (unlike math or coding contests) ... Setting up thousands of Docker images is an infrastructural nightmare ... Observation: strong models can solve many tasks without execution feedback ... Key: strong models have internal "world model" of code semantics ... SWE-Zero: 300K agent trajectories that don't require repository-specific execution ... 150K GitHub PRs ... OpenHands scaffold, remove future git commits to prevent "git hacking" by agent
Distilled from Qwen3-Coder-480B + filtering (try to execute anyway) ... SWE-Hero: 13K agent trajectories that do require execution feedback
21K interactive Python SWE tasks from 3.4K GitHub repositories ... 450K PRs from GitHub and GitHub Archive ... Used Qwen 2.5-72B-Instruct to install dependencies and assess PR quality

Scale SWE-Zero up to 12M agent trajectories ... Used the SWE-rebench-v2 tasks (32K executable tasks + 120K nonexecutable tasks) ... Ran mini-coder-1.7b (very small model, 50.4 pass@100), mini-swe-agent scaffold
Code environments are painful ... Lots of filtering and other details

anchors.ref: paper linked at L425; figure shown at L426
paper linked at L430; figures shown at L434, L439, L442
paper linked at L444; figure shown at L448
dataset linked at L450; example row linked at L454

anchors.quote: So this SWE-smith paper had the idea of-- you're given a repository, you're using a language model to automatically generate tasks. ... So these are synthetic tasks, but you get 50k of them
unlike math, SWE tasks have a lot of heavy dependencies. ... Most GitHub repos like don't even run. ... And this is just a nightmare.

they noticed that the models are actually good enough that they can solve a lot of these tasks without execution feedback. ... If you don't allow execution, you get almost 70, which is not bad for not being able to execute code. ... So somehow these models have some internal semantics of code.

There's a lot of details how to prevent agent hacking. ... You can only do set, grep, and all these basic operations. ... filtered because sometimes the Qwen model will ignore these instructions and still try to execute anyway.

oh, they also had a 13k agent trajectories that do require execution feedback. ... So they train models where they first fine-tune on these SWE-Zero examples, and then fine-tune again on these SWE-Zero examples.

So you can take this SWE-Zero idea, and you can now scale up to 12 million agent trajectories. ... The nice benefit of SWE-Zero is that it's very lightweight. ... But SWE-Zero doesn't care. ... You can use all of them.

The result figures (swezero-noexec.png, swezero-results.png, swe-rebench.png) are shown and not restated; in particular the fraction of tasks solvable without execution lives only in the L434 image. 'Git hacking' (L438) is the professor's term for an agent reading the repository's future commits to find the fix; this thread treats it as the named failure mode of giving agents a real repo history. The 'try to execute anyway' filter (L440) means non-executing trajectories were still checked by execution where possible; the professor gives no pass rate. Correction (1:21:05-1:21:17): the note reads the 'try to execute anyway' filter (L440) as non-executing trajectories being 'still checked by execution where possible'. Aloud the filter removes trajectories in which the Qwen teacher 'will ignore these instructions and still try to execute anyway', i.e. it enforces the no-execution protocol (the SWE-Zero agent may use only sed- and grep-style commands, 1:20:52-1:20:58, captioned 'set, grep'). The earlier reading is withdrawn as this thread's misreading. Figure read aloud (1:20:01-1:20:08): with execution 'you get 80', without 'almost 70' (swezero-noexec.png; quoted, not restated as this thread's). Git hacking: aloud only 'a lot of details how to prevent agent hacking' (1:20:41); removing future commits (L438) is never explained aloud, so the gloss stays this thread's. Spoken evidence: why execution is dropped: 'Most GitHub repos like don't even run' and old dependencies make it 'a nightmare' (1:19:25-1:19:36); lightweight SWE-Zero can use all of SWE-rebench's non-executable tasks, which execution-based pipelines must discard (1:22:36-1:22:46). Not imported. Imprecision (1:22:06): SWE-rebench uses 'a language model to give you the responses'; L447 says the LM installs dependencies and assesses PR quality.
